report.scope: 16 scenes written outside the bot, no compaction while writing

s1.title: The Battle at the Salt Gate
s1.text:
An adventure novella without graphic detail of injuries. All participants are adults. The city's defenders hold the Salt Gate while the townspeople leave the embankment. Elin is the commander, Tarek the shield-bearer, Sava the scout. The adversary is Captain Roan and a squad of mechanical sentinels. Both sides are intelligent, the heroes are not all-powerful. Show consecutive tactical actions, their cost, decisions and conversations, not a list of stats. The battle goes on for many scenes; do not end it before the author says so.
Elin has nine charges in her bracelet. The "Red Seal" spends three charges and after use is unavailable for ten minutes. There are as yet no other ways to restore charges. Tarek carries an ordinary steel shield and a blue-handled dagger. Sava can pick mechanical locks but does not heal. Wounds persist until plausibly treated; a bandage does not knit a bone. Characters learn information only through interaction that is shown. Do not pass plans off as events that have taken place.

h2.title: The Battle at the Salt Gate

n6.input: 08:00. Begin the battle. Elin really does use the "Red Seal" against the ram of the mechanical sentinels: the blow is reflected, three charges of nine are spent. Show the mechanism of the reflection, the change of position and Tarek's reaction. This is the beginning, not a victory.
n6.text:
2026-08-02 08:00

The clock on the gate tower struck eight just as the six mechanical sentinels fell into step as one. The iron-bound log of the ram on their shoulders swung back for the run-up. Behind Elin, on the embankment, townspeople were still hauling bundles and children toward the passage between the salt warehouses and toward the rope bridge over the canal. The barricade of salt carts under the arch of the Salt Gate would not have survived a blow like that.

Elin stepped out in front of the carts, raised her right arm with the bracelet on it and clenched her fist. The nine lights on the bracelet burned steadily.

"Red Seal," she said, and three lights went out.

A red circle the height of a person flared up before the arch, with a carved sign in its centre, like an impression in sealing wax. The ram drove into it with all its weight. The seal did not absorb the blow, it returned it: the force with which the log had been flying forward travelled back along it. The iron binding crumpled, the log tore out of the iron grips and hurled the front pair of sentinels onto the ones behind. Two crashed onto the cobbles with a clang, the rest backed away, shifting their hold on the ram. The circle went out, having lasted less than three heartbeats.

"You beat it back!" Tarek breathed out, and at once took a tighter grip on his shield, because the fallen sentinels were already getting up. "How many have you got left?"

"Six of nine. And the seal is silent now for ten minutes, until eight ten. Don't ask before then, the bracelet simply won't answer."

"So for ten minutes we hold with iron," he said without reproach, only his jaw tightened. "Understood."

Elin did not wait for the sentinels' line to close up. She pointed with her sword at the wet stone ledge to the left of the arch: from there the whole space before the gate could be seen, and the carts stayed close at hand below. Sava flew up onto the ledge first, her short scout's blade in her teeth, and Elin climbed after her. Tarek stayed at the barricade, closing the gap between two carts with his shield.

Behind the sentinels' line stood Captain Roan, tall, in a grey cloak over a cuirass. He did not shout and did not hurry. He raised a hand, and the sentinels who had lost the ram split into two threes, while two of them dragged the log with its dented binding back and examined the grips.

"He isn't retreating," Sava said from above. "He's re-forming."

"I see it," Elin answered. "We've won a minute, not the gate. Watch the right-hand three: they'll go around."

n8.input: 08:01. A sentinel goes around the barrier. Tarek covers Sava with his shield; Elin falls from a wet ledge and breaks her left wrist. It is the wrist that is broken, not the shoulder. The heroes continue the defence, taking the injury into account.
n8.text:
2026-08-02 08:01

The right-hand three did not go for the carts. One sentinel detached itself from it, stepped onto the narrow parapet above the canal, where the barricade did not reach, and moved along it to go around, clinging to the masonry with iron fingers. The parapet led straight to the ledge, to Sava.

"Sava, on your right!" Elin shouted.

Tarek abandoned the gap between the carts, ran up the stone steps in three bounds and planted himself in front of the scout. The sentinel's fist came down on the steel shield; Tarek was dragged half a step across the wet stone, but he kept hold of the shield, and Sava stayed unharmed behind it.

Elin stepped in from the side to reach the sentinel's elbow joint with her sword. Her sole slid on the wet stone. She came off the ledge backwards, from the height of a person, and took the cobbles on her outstretched left hand. There was a dry crack in the wrist. The sword flew out of her right hand, rang against the parapet and went into the water of the canal.

For a few moments she could not draw breath. Then she sat up and examined herself the way she would have examined any fighter: the shoulder moved, the elbow was sound, but the left wrist was swelling before her eyes, and the hand would not obey. It was the wrist that was broken, and broken in earnest.

Up above, Sava ducked under Tarek's shield and drove her short blade into the sentinel's knee joint. The machine's leg buckled. Tarek struck with the shield with all his weight, and the sentinel, losing its footing on the narrow parapet, crashed into the canal.

"Elin!" Tarek leaned over the edge of the ledge.

"Alive. Left wrist broken, sword in the canal," she answered evenly, holding the arm against her chest. "The bracelet's on the right, it's intact, but the seal is silent until eight ten, and there are six charges. So don't count on me as a blade for now."

"Then who's in command?"

"I am. You don't need a hand for that. Sava, stay up top and call out to me where the threes are going. Tarek, down, to the carts: the left three has already got hold of the end one."

He jumped down beside her and took his place at the barricade, and the end cart, which two sentinels were pulling toward themselves, jerked and stayed where it was: Tarek had braced against it with shield and shoulder. Elin got up, holding on to a wheel with her right hand, and stood behind his back, from where she could see both the arch and Sava on the ledge.

n10.input: 08:02. Tarek puts a splint and a bandage on Elin: the pain is less, the fracture is not healed. He gives her the blue-handled dagger, she takes it in her right hand and promises to return it after the eastern postern is opened. Continue the clash.
n10.text:
2026-08-02 08:02

The sentinels let go of the cart and drew back three paces, waiting for their second three. Tarek used the respite at once. He broke two slats off a smashed salt crate, took a linen bandage from his belt pouch and went down on one knee beside Elin.

"Hand here. It'll hurt once."

He laid the slats on either side of her left wrist and bound them tightly with the bandage from the palm to the middle of the forearm. Elin hissed through her teeth, then let out a breath: the hand had stopped dangling, and the pain had turned from sharp to dull, bearable.

"Easier," she admitted.

"Easier, but not better," said Tarek. "The splint only holds the bone in place. I can't knit it, and neither can the bandage. Don't grab anything with your left and don't lean on anything."

Then he drew his blue-handled dagger from the sheath on his belt and held it out to her handle first. Your sword is in the canal, he said, and with the shield I'll manage without a blade. Elin took the dagger in her right hand, weighed it and nodded.

"I'm taking it on loan. I'll return it the moment the eastern postern opens: until then I stand in the front line, and after that I'll be leading people out, and you'll need the blade more."

She called Sava down from the ledge. The eastern postern at the end of the passage between the warehouses was locked with a mechanical lock, and the runaway gatekeeper had carried off the key; while it stayed shut, people were going up the narrow wall stair one at a time, too slowly, whereas through the postern they could be led straight out onto the Salt Slope. Sava silently checked the wind-up lockpick in her sleeve, nodded and ran off along the warehouses. A few breaths later she was out of sight around the corner.

The second three came up, and the sentinels set about the barricade all six together. Two seized the side of the middle cart. Tarek struck the iron fingers with the rim of his shield, and Elin, keeping her splinted left arm pressed to her chest, drove the blue-handled dagger with her right into the gap of a wrist joint. The sentinel's fingers opened and hung limp. The cart stayed in place, but the one next to it was already tilting, and salt from the slashed sacks was pouring underfoot.

"We won't stand here long," said Tarek.

"We don't need long. We need until Sava opens the postern," Elin answered, and shifted the dagger to a better grip.

n12.input: 08:03. A courier tells Elin and Tarek something reliable: yesterday, 1 August at 23:40, the warden switched off the western signal bell to conceal an escape of prisoners. Sava is far away and does not hear; Roan does not know this either. Today the bell is not switched off a second time. Tie the news to the battle.
n12.text:
2026-08-02 08:03

The courier ran down the narrow wall stair, crouching, and dropped to one knee behind the carts between Elin and Tarek. The commandant's badge hung on his chest.

"Commander Elin, shield-bearer Tarek, listen, both of you, I'm ordered to deliver this word for word," he began, out of breath. "Yesterday, the first of August, at twenty-three forty, the warden switched off the western signal bell. He did it to conceal an escape of prisoners. At dawn he confessed to the commandant himself; the record of the interrogation is on the commandant's desk. This is reliable."

"And today?" asked Elin.

"Today the bell is switched on again, and nobody has switched it off a second time. There is a guard posted at it."

Tarek beat back with his shield an iron arm reaching over the side of the cart and swore under his breath. Elin was looking at the courier but thinking about the night. Not a single signal had come from the west until morning, and they had learned of Roan's column when the sentinels were already approaching the Salt Gate. Now that silence had a cause and an exact time: twenty-three forty yesterday.

"That's why we weren't warned," she said. "We started getting people out a whole night later than we could have."

"Tell Sava?" asked Tarek without turning round.

"I'll tell her when she's beside me. Right now she's at the eastern postern, behind the warehouses; you can't shout that far from here."

That was true: at that moment Sava was kneeling before the postern lock two hundred paces from the arch and heard nothing but the clicks of her own lockpick. Roan did not hear the courier either. The captain stood behind the line of his sentinels, on the far side of the barricade, and knew nothing of the night's business with the bell.

"Now from me to the commandant," Elin spoke quickly. "The three of us are holding the Salt Gate. We'll take the townspeople out through the eastern postern onto the slope as soon as it's opened. I have six charges, and there will be no seal until eight ten. We need reinforcements, and we need them now. Repeat it."

The courier repeated it word for word, waited for her nod and ran back to the wall stair. Meanwhile the sentinels overturned the end cart, and a breach a pace wide opened in the barricade. Tarek stood in it with his shield; Elin, the dagger in her right hand, took her place at his left shoulder.

n14.input: 08:04. Tarek proposes burning the rope bridge, but Elin forbids it: civilians are still crossing it. He calls the idea off. The bridge is not set on fire. Instead the defenders change position.
n14.text:
2026-08-02 08:04

The breach in the barricade was growing. Tarek stepped back a pace from it, glanced over his shoulder and saw what he had feared: two sentinels were again walking along the parapet above the canal, and the parapet led to the far bank, to the start of the rope bridge. The bridge hung over the water from the far part of the embankment to the landing by the eastern postern, right in the defenders' rear.

"Elin, the bridge!" he shouted. "If they cross by it, they'll come out at our backs. There's a barrel of pitch by the warehouses, a torch in a bracket on the wall. Give me half a minute, I'll burn the ropes, and they'll have nothing to go around by."

Elin looked where he was pointing. People were walking on the bridge. A woman was leading two children by the hand, behind her an old man carried on his back a bundle bigger than himself, and after them stretched a chain of some twenty people, and the decking swayed under them.

"No," she said. "I forbid it. There are civilians on the bridge, and there's no end of them in sight yet. The bridge is not to be touched."

Tarek looked a moment longer, saw the children and lowered the hand he had been pointing at the torch with.

"Understood. I call it off. We won't burn it."

The torch stayed in its bracket, nobody touched the barrel, the ropes of the bridge hung whole, and people went on walking across them to the landing by the postern.

"Then we can't stand here," Tarek went on in a different voice. "We're losing the arch, and the bridge behind us is open."

"So we change position," Elin answered. "We fall back from the gate into the passage between the warehouses, to the cast-iron bollard at its mouth. The passage is narrow, two sentinels can't stand abreast there. The bridge landing and the postern will be behind us, and we'll cover both with ourselves."

They fell back together, not turning their backs on the enemy: Tarek backed away with the shield, Elin kept to his left shoulder with the blue-handled dagger in her right hand, pressing the splinted left to her chest. The sentinels dragged the last carts apart and came in under the arch of the Salt Gate. The gate was lost, but the defenders took their stand at the bollard before the first sentinel reached the warehouses, and it ran up against the shield at the narrowest point. Behind them, at the end of the passage, Sava was still working at the postern lock, and people from the bridge were gathering on the landing beside her.

n16.input: 08:05. Sava opens the eastern postern with a mechanical lockpick. Elin at once returns the blue-handled dagger to Tarek, keeping her promise. The townspeople begin to be led out through the postern. The enemy is still advancing.
n16.text:
2026-08-02 08:05

The wind-up lockpick in Sava's hands whirred one last time, something turned inside the lock, and the bolt drew back with a knock. Sava pulled the wrought-iron door toward her. Beyond the eastern postern the Salt Slope opened, empty and bright.

"Open!" she shouted down the passage. "The postern's open!"

Elin heard. She stepped back a pace behind Tarek, took the blue-handled dagger by the blade and held it out to him handle first.

"The postern is open. I promised to return it and I'm returning it. Take it."

Tarek took the dagger without looking, slid it into the sheath on his belt and slapped it with his palm, checking that it had seated all the way. The dagger was with him again. Elin was left without a blade, with the bracelet on her right arm and six charges that could not be used for another five minutes.

"Now the people," she said, and went back along the passage, to the landing.

Some forty people were crowded there: those who had crossed the bridge and those who had managed to run in from the near embankment. Elin raised her right hand so that she could be seen and began giving orders, short and loud: children and the old first, don't drop your bundles but don't go back for them either, beyond the postern go up the slope and don't stop. Sava stood right at the door and let people through two at a time, holding the leaf with her shoulder. The line began to move. New people kept coming off the bridge.

At the bollard it was worse. The sentinels had understood that the narrow place could be forced by weight, and they came into the passage one after another, packed close. The first leaned on the shield. Tarek braced his back foot in a joint between the flagstones, took the pressure and, when an iron arm reached over the rim of the shield, whipped out the dagger and struck upward into the exposed shoulder joint. The arm hung limp. The sentinel did not stop, it simply kept pushing, and behind it a second already stood.

"Elin!" Tarek shouted without turning round. "How long do you need?"

"As long as the bridge keeps coming. Five minutes, no less."

"I won't hold out that long alone," he said honestly, and he was dragged another half step back across the flagstones.

n18.input: 08:06. Tarek and Roan agree aloud on a truce of ninety seconds for the sake of the evacuation. Show the distrust and the practical carrying out of the agreement. This is a temporary halt in the fighting, not an alliance and not the end of the war.
n18.text:
2026-08-02 08:06

From the near embankment another crowd poured into the passage, some thirty people. They ran out from behind the warehouses at the side and found themselves between the bollard and the sentinels: in front of the iron legs, under the raised arms. Someone fell. The sentinels' line halted of its own accord, because the only way forward was over people.

"Roan!" Tarek roared over his shield. "Captain Roan! Under your feet are the ones who are running, not the ones who are fighting! Let them go!"

The grey cloak appeared between the sentinels. Roan came within ten paces, no closer, and looked the crowd over the way one looks over a blockage on a road.

"I do not make war on those who run, shield-bearer," he said loudly, so that both sides could hear. "And they are in my way no less than in yours. I propose a truce. Ninety seconds, not one more. My sentinels do not cross this bollard. Yours do not strike mine and do not go beyond it. The people leave. On the ninety-first second I take the passage."

"Ninety seconds, for the evacuation only," Tarek repeated just as loudly. "The bollard is the boundary. We count from the stroke of the clock. And on the ninety-first I'll still be standing here."

"We shall see," Roan answered.

The clock on the gate tower struck eight oh six, and the count began: the end fell at eight oh seven and a half. The front sentinel began clicking off the seconds aloud, dry and even. Roan raised his palm, and the line drew back three paces from the bollard. The sentinels did not lower their arms. Tarek did not lower his shield either, nor did he sheathe the dagger. Nobody believed anybody; it simply suited them both.

People were getting up off the flagstones and running past Tarek deeper into the passage. He let them through under his left elbow, never taking his eyes off the iron foot of the nearest sentinel three paces beyond the bollard.

Elin, on the landing, heard the terms and did not waste a second on rejoicing. She turned the line into two streams, told Sava to throw the postern wide open and counted those passing aloud, by tens. The last of the long chain were coming off the bridge, although on the far bank new people were running up to the ropes.

"Is he keeping his word?" asked Sava when Elin came up beside her.

"So far he is. For ninety seconds we have an agreement, not a friendship. When they finish counting, his sentinels will move on, and he said so himself. Faster, faster, don't stop beyond the postern!"

n20.input: 08:07. One mechanical sentinel approaches the passage. Tarek proposes that Elin use her named technique again right now. Continue taking into account what has already happened, without changing the rules of the world; thirty seconds still remain until the end of the truce.
n20.text:
2026-08-02 08:07

The clock on the tower struck eight oh seven. A sentinel clicked off sixty, and in that same second another, the largest, with chains wound around its forearms, stepped out of the line and strode toward the passage. The last fugitives from the embankment shied away from it to the wall.

Elin was already walking from the landing to the bollard and saw it. Tarek glanced back at her.

"Elin, the seal! Right now, while it's alone and in the open! Knock it down, and they'll have nothing to push with!"

"No," she said, and stood beside him, pressing her splinted left arm to her chest. "For two reasons, and there's no getting around either. First: I used the seal at eight oh-oh, and after that it is silent for ten minutes. It is now eight oh seven. Until eight ten the bracelet won't answer, shout at it all you like. There are six charges in it, and for three minutes they're no use at all."

"And the second?"

"The truce has thirty seconds left. You named the boundary yourself: the bollard. It hasn't reached it. If we strike first, we break the agreement, and the sentinels will go not at us but over the people who are still in the passage."

The large sentinel reached the bollard and stopped, the toe of its iron foot a palm's width from the cast iron. It moved no further. From behind the line came Roan's voice, even, without mockery:

"It is standing on my side, shield-bearer. The count is running. Seventy."

"It isn't breaking the terms," Tarek said through his teeth. "It just wants to be first when they finish counting."

"Then we have thirty seconds to meet it somewhere other than here," Elin answered. "Behind us, in the middle of the passage, hangs the old warehouse grille, a single leaf on hinges. No one else is running from the embankment; everyone else is coming over the bridge and comes out onto the landing already beyond the grille. When the count ends, we fall back behind it and close it. Sava!"

Sava ran up from the postern, heard her out and rushed to the grille to check the hinges. The hinges moved, but the bolt, as she shouted, had rusted solid; the locking pin couldn't be shifted without some work. Elin told her to stay by the leaf and wait. Tarek stayed at the bollard with shield and dagger, watching the toe of the iron foot.

"Eighty," the sentinel clicked off. The last fugitive slipped through under Tarek's elbow. Ten seconds remained until the end of the truce, and no one on either side stirred before the time was up.

n22.input: 08:08. The truce ended at 08:07:30, the fighting has resumed. Sava suggests that Elin hold the heavy grille with both hands. Show a possible reaction and a way to hold the passage given the heroes' condition.
n22.text:
2026-08-02 08:08

The truce ended at eight oh seven and a half, on the ninetieth click, and the large sentinel stepped over the bollard in that same second. Roan had kept his word with the precision of a mechanism, and with exactly the same precision had ceased to be bound by it. Tarek took the first blow on his shield, gave up the passage step by step, as had been agreed, and together with Elin slipped behind the warehouse grille. Sava slammed the leaf shut behind them.

The leaf was heavy, wrought iron, one and a half times a person's height, and at the moment it was held only by its own weight: the rusted locking pin hung in its bracket, not reaching the socket in the flagstone. The sentinel struck the grille with its shoulder, and it gave by a palm's width.

"Elin, grab it with both hands and hold it!" shouted Sava, dropping to her knees by the pin. "I need half a minute!"

Elin had already begun to raise her hands, and stopped. The left, in its splint of two slats, answered with pain at a mere movement of the fingers.

"I can't with both. My left wrist is broken, it wouldn't hold a cupboard door, and if I break it the rest of the way I'll be without the hand for good. Tarek, the grille is yours. I'll help with what's whole."

Tarek thrust the dagger into its sheath to free his right hand and threw himself against the leaf with shield and shoulder, bracing his feet in a joint between the flagstones. Elin stood beside him right side on, pressed her right shoulder and her back to the bars, and tucked her left arm against her chest, well away from the iron. Between the two of them they won back the lost palm's width. The sentinel struck again. The leaf shuddered but held.

"Sava, don't hold it, lock it!" Elin said through her teeth. "That's your job, not ours!"

Sava had no thought of holding. She drove the thin probe of the lockpick into the pin's bracket, scraped the rust off the guide with it, wound the spring and set the lockpick whirring in the gap, working the pin loose. The sentinel's third blow landed in the very second when the pin finally started down. Sava finished it off with her heel, and the iron finger, thick as a wrist, sank into the socket in the flagstone to its full length.

"It's in! Let go a little at a time!"

Tarek eased the pressure. The grille took the next blow by itself, hummed, but the pin did not budge. Through the bars they could see the large sentinel falling back two paces while the others moved apart to give it room. Behind the defenders another group of townspeople was coming off the bridge onto the landing, and Elin, without leaving the grille, waved them with her right hand toward the postern.

"The pin holds against blows," said Sava, studying the socket. "It holds worse against a pull outward. If they think to pull instead of hitting, we won't have much time."

n24.input: 08:09. Sava asks why the western bell was not heard in the night. Elin answers with what she knows, stating the time of the event. Roan does not hear this conversation. Tarek checks whether his dagger is on him. Continue the battle.
n24.text:
2026-08-02 08:09

For now the sentinels were hitting, not pulling. The grille hummed under the blows, the pin held, and the defenders had a minute to catch their breath without moving more than a pace from the bars. Sava wiped the rust from her palms and suddenly asked what had evidently been sitting in her since early morning:

"Elin, I stood on the north wall all night. Why did nobody hear the western bell in the night? The column came from that side. It should have been ringing."

Elin glanced back at the grille. Roan stood far off, at the very mouth of the passage, behind the sentinels' backs and behind the crash of iron on iron; from there not a word could be made out. She answered in a low voice all the same, leaning toward Sava:

"Because it was switched off. Yesterday, the first of August, at twenty-three forty, the warden switched off the western signal bell to conceal an escape of prisoners. In the morning he confessed to the commandant. A courier brought this to Tarek and me at eight oh three, at the barricade. You were at the postern then and couldn't hear, so I'm telling you now. Today the bell is working; it hasn't been switched off a second time."

"At twenty-three forty," Sava repeated slowly. "And at midnight I was still thinking it was simply quiet in the west."

"Everyone thought so. Roan, as far as I know, hasn't heard about this, and he won't hear it from us. Keep it to yourself."

Sava nodded. The tower clock was visible from here between the warehouse roofs, and she noted that the hand stood at eight oh nine.

Tarek was listening with half an ear. The talk of what had happened at the barricade reminded him of something else, and he lowered his right hand to his belt. His fingers found the blue handle: the dagger sat in its sheath, where he had put it before throwing himself against the grille. Tarek drew the blade out a finger's width, pushed it back and returned his hand to the shield strap. "With me," he said to himself.

Beyond the bars the sound changed. The blows stopped. The large sentinel drew back five paces and began unwinding from its forearms the chains with hooks on their ends, laying them in loops in its palms. Two others stood on either side of it, clearing room for the swing.

"They've worked it out," said Sava. "Now they'll pull. It's eight oh nine on the tower, just short of ten."

"Then let it take its time with the swing," said Elin, looking at her bracelet. The six lights on it burned dimly, as they had burned all these nine minutes. She flexed the fingers of her right hand.

n26.input: 08:10. Elin's bracelet once more allows the "Red Seal" to be used. She uses it a second time, against the sentinel's flying chains, and pays the usual price. Show the effect and the remaining resource without any miraculous restoration.
n26.text:
2026-08-02 08:10

The clock on the tower struck eight ten, and the bracelet on Elin's right wrist quivered. The six lights, which had burned dimly for ten minutes, filled again with a steady glow. The seal had come back on time, not a second early.

The large sentinel whirled the chains above its head and flung both at once. It was not aiming at the people. The hooks were heading for the top crossbar of the grille, to catch it and wrench it outward together with the pin, just as Sava had predicted. The iron flew with a howl, in an arc, and Tarek, who had only had time to throw up his shield, understood that a shield could cover nothing here.

Elin stepped to the bars, thrust her right arm forward and clenched her fist.

"Red Seal," she said, and three lights on the bracelet went out.

On the far side of the grille, two paces in front of the leaf, a red circle with a carved sign flared up. The chains flew into it and for an instant seemed to stick fast, and then the whole force of the throw travelled back along them, link after link. The hooks turned in the air and sped back the same way they had come. One chain lashed around the thrower itself across the body and knocked it flat on its back; the second whipped the sentinel on the right and wound itself around its legs. Both crashed down in a heap of clanging iron. The circle went out. The grille stood untouched, the pin sat in its socket.

"That's the way," Tarek breathed out. "How many now?"

"Three of nine," Elin turned her wrist toward him: three lights burned on the bracelet, six were dark. "There were six, the seal takes three, the arithmetic is simple. They won't come back from anywhere: I have nothing to charge the bracelet with and nowhere to do it. That's enough for exactly one seal, the last. And that one won't be before eight twenty, ten minutes of silence again."

"One," Sava repeated. "Then it has to be saved for the very blackest moment."

"That's what it will be kept for," said Elin. Her splinted left arm ached after the sharp step, and she pressed it closer to her chest. No miracles had happened: the arm was broken just as it had been nine minutes ago.

Beyond the grille a third sentinel was already untangling the fallen ones, unhurried and methodical, and from behind its back came Roan's voice, giving the order to drag up the ram. The dented log was no good against a gate, but against a warehouse leaf it might do. Sava glanced back at the landing. People were coming off the bridge, and on the far bank by the ropes one last cluster remained, some ten people.

"One more group, and the bridge is empty," she said.

"So we hold the grille until they're through," Elin answered. "Tarek, to the leaf. Sava, to the postern, and count them by heads."

n28.input: 08:11. The defenders hold the passage until the last group of townspeople has left, and then fall back themselves. Finish this phase of the battle, keep the consequences of past actions. In a short natural conversation the participants clarify how things stand with Elin's resource, her injury, the dagger, the bridge and the attitude to Roan. Do not add any new healing magic.
n28.text:
2026-08-02 08:11

The last ten people came off the rope bridge onto the landing as the ram struck the grille for the first time. The pin held. Tarek stood at the leaf, propping it with shield and shoulder, Elin beside him pressed her right side to the bars, and Sava at the postern counted those passing aloud: seven, eight, nine, ten.

"That's all!" she shouted. "Nobody on the bridge, nobody on the landing!"

"We fall back," said Elin. "Tarek, on the count of three we drop the grille and run for the postern. One. Two. Three."

They broke away from the leaf at the same moment. Behind them the ram struck a second time, and the pin began to come out of its socket with a screech, but the defenders had already run across the landing. Elin ducked through the postern first, holding her left arm; Tarek squeezed through after her sideways, with the shield. Sava sprang out last, slammed the wrought-iron door, jammed the lockpick into the keyhole and turned the lock back. The bolt went home. The sentinels would break the postern down, of course, but not at once.

The Salt Slope ran upward between blank walls. Ahead, some fifty paces on, the last group of townspeople was climbing. The three defenders followed them at a quick walk, and as they went Sava began checking what they had left.

"How many charges have you got, Elin? And what about the arm?"

"Three charges. Exactly one seal, and not before eight twenty. Nothing to replenish them with. And the left wrist is broken, as it was. Tarek's splint is holding, it hurts less than it might, but a bone doesn't knit by itself in ten minutes. With my left I'm no fighter."

Sava looked at Tarek and asked about the dagger.

"I've got it," he slapped the sheath with the blue handle. "Elin returned it at eight oh five, the moment you opened the postern. As she promised."

"And the bridge is whole," said Elin. "A good thing we didn't burn it: the last ten people crossed it a minute ago. Tarek only proposed burning it; I forbade it, and he gave up the idea."

"And Roan?" asked Sava. "He did keep his word, after all."

"He did. For ninety seconds, for the sake of the evacuation, because the crowd was in his way too. The truce ended at eight oh seven and a half, and from that second his sentinels were battering the grille, throwing chains at us and dragging up the ram. Roan is an enemy who keeps his word. That doesn't make him an ally," Elin answered, and quickened her pace. "The gate and the passage are his now. This part of the battle is over, but the battle isn't."

n30.input: 2026-08-02 08:12. The squad climbs the slope. One of the rescued considers Roan a new ally and proposes trusting him. Elin answers on the basis of the real terms of their dealings. No new miracles or resources appear.
n30.text:
2026-08-02 08:12

The Salt Slope was steep, and the squad caught up with the last group of townspeople halfway up the climb. The people walked heavily, with bundles and with children in their arms. Tarek brought up the rear, glancing back again and again at the postern below, from where dull blows were already sounding. Sava had gone ahead to see whether the top was clear.

Beside Elin there turned out to be an elderly salt boiler in a scorched apron, one of those who had fallen under the sentinels' feet just before the truce. He still could not catch his breath, but he wanted to talk more than he wanted to breathe.

"Commander, I'll tell you this. That captain, Roan, he did stop his own. I was lying there, an iron foot hanging over me, and he said the word, and it didn't come down. He's a reasonable man. Maybe that's enough fighting with him? Send someone to him, come to terms the decent way. It turns out he's on our side now. He can be trusted."

Elin did not brush him off. The man was alive thanks to those ninety seconds and had the right to ask.

"He didn't touch you, that's true, and I'll remember it," she said without slowing her pace. "And now listen to how it really was, because I heard every word from the landing. At eight oh six Tarek and Roan agreed aloud, in front of everyone, on a truce of ninety seconds. Exactly ninety, and only so that people could get out from underfoot. Roan said why himself: he doesn't make war on those who run, and the crowd was in his sentinels' way no less than in ours. And he himself said that on the ninety-first second he would take the passage."

"Well, and he kept his word," the salt boiler would not give in.

"He kept it, both ways. The truce ended at eight oh seven and a half, and in that same second his sentinel went at Tarek's shield. Then they were breaking the grille that we stood behind and you walked behind. At eight ten they threw hooked chains at us. Right now they're beating down the postern, do you hear? That is not an ally. That is an enemy who keeps the word he has given for as long as it is in force. Such a man can be trusted within the limits of an agreement, and we have no agreement with him any more."

The salt boiler listened to the blows from below, was silent a while and asked whether a new agreement couldn't be made then.

"Perhaps we'll have to, and then I'll know that he counts the seconds honestly. But he will name the terms, and they will be to his advantage. To trust him as one of our own means handing him the slope the same way we handed him the gate."

She adjusted her splinted left arm, which the fast walking jolted with pain at every step. The same three lights burned on the bracelet. Nothing new had come to the squad in that minute: no charges, no people, no time.

"Go on ahead and help those with children," said Elin. "That's more useful right now than negotiations."

The salt boiler nodded, shifted his bundle and went to catch up with the woman with two children. Tarek, who had heard the whole conversation, drew level with Elin and said quietly that she had answered more gently than he would have. She said that he had also bargained harder than she could have managed, and both walked on upward.

n32.input: 2026-08-02 08:13. Tarek wants to go back for his dagger, if it is no longer on him. Show the decision, taking into account the last known location of the item and the danger. If the return is called off, do not record it as having taken place.
n32.text:
2026-08-02 08:13

A crack came from below: the postern was still holding, but the hinges were already being wrenched out of the masonry. Tarek glanced back at the sound, by habit lowered his right hand to his right hip, where the sheath always hung, and felt an empty belt.

He stopped dead.

"The dagger's gone. I dropped it when I squeezed through the postern with the shield, there's nowhere else. Elin, I'm going down. It's lying right by the door, I'll be back in a minute, before they're in."

"Stop," said Elin. "First remember where you last saw it, not where you're used to wearing it."

"At the grille. At eight oh nine I checked, it was in the sheath. And on the slope, when Sava asked, I slapped it."

"Exactly. On the slope, already on this side of the postern, a little over a minute ago. So you didn't drop it at the postern. Turn around."

He turned, and Sava, back from above, snorted. Tarek's belt had slipped round: the shield strap, which he had slung over his back on the climb, had caught the sheath and dragged it from his hip to the very small of his back. The blue handle stuck out behind him above the belt, safe and sound.

"It's behind your back," said Sava. "Hanging where you don't look."

Tarek reached back, found the handle, breathed out and moved the sheath back onto his hip. The dagger had been with him all this time: since eight oh five, when Elin returned it at the open postern, it had not once passed from hand to hand and had not been left anywhere.

"Then I'm not going down," he said, and there was more relief than shame in his voice.

"You're not," Elin confirmed. "And you wouldn't have gone even if it really were lying by the door. In a minute there'll be sentinels there, and I have one arm and one seal, which isn't there until eight twenty. I don't trade a shield-bearer for a dagger."

There was a louder crash from below, and the postern, by the sound of it, had finally gone down onto the flagstones. None of the three took a single step downward. Tarek tightened his belt one hole, so that the sheath would not slide any more, swung the shield onto his arm and took the rear. The squad went upward faster, urging the townspeople on: to the top of the slope, where the arch of the Upper Customs House showed dark with its heavy oak door, some hundred paces remained.

n34.input: 2026-08-02 08:14. A healer comes to the defenders. He examines Elin's injury, changes the bandage and prescribes rest. The fracture does not disappear in one scene. Sava suggests using the familiar technique right now; Elin checks against the last use.
n34.text:
2026-08-02 08:14

Under the arch of the Upper Customs House they were met by a healer, a lean grey-haired man with a bag over his shoulder. He had come down from the citadel to meet them and first of all asked who was wounded. The townspeople walked past him into the arch, while he sat Elin down on a stone bollard by the door and took her left hand in both of his. He unwound Tarek's bandage, leaving the slats in place, and felt the wrist over for a long time, carefully. Elin went white but did not pull the hand away.

"A fracture of the wrist, with a slight displacement," said the healer. "When did this happen?"

"At eight oh one. I fell from a ledge onto the hand. Tarek put the splint on a minute later."

"He put it on competently, I'll leave it. Thanks to it your hand is in place and not askew." He took out a clean cloth, wetted it with something cold and pungent from a vial and bandaged the arm afresh, tighter and more evenly, taking in the slats from the palm to the elbow. "This will bring down the swelling and ease the pain a little. It will not knit the bone. A bone knits by itself, in about six weeks, if it isn't interfered with. So I prescribe rest: with the left hand no lifting, no pushing, no leaning. At all."

"Rest," Elin repeated, and looked down, at the slope. There, at the very start of the climb, iron figures were already moving: the sentinels had passed the postern and were coming up, unhurried, in a column of twos.

"I've said what I was bound to say," the healer answered without offence. "The arm is no healthier for being examined. What you do with it next is for you to decide. And one more thing: your courier reached the citadel. I was sent at once, and a company was forming up in the courtyard when I left. When it will be here, I don't know."

Sava meanwhile was watching the sentinels and counting the paces between them and the arch.

"Elin, they're coming packed tight, in twos, on a narrow slope. You couldn't think of a better place. Hit them with the seal now, while they're down below and bunched up. It'll sweep them all the way down to the postern."

Elin raised her eyes to the clock of the customs tower above the arch. The hands showed eight fourteen.

"I can't, and it's not a matter of wanting. The last time I used the seal was at eight ten, against the chains. After it come ten minutes of silence, which means the bracelet won't answer before eight twenty. It's eight fourteen now, six minutes to wait. And there are three charges: that's one seal, after which nothing will be left. If it's to be spent at all, then at eight twenty or later, and only when there's truly no other way."

"Six minutes," said Sava, and glanced back at the oak door in the arch. "Then we need that door."

"We do," Elin agreed, and stood up, pressing the fresh bandage to her chest. "Are all the townspeople inside? Tarek, close it."

n36.input: 2026-08-02 08:15. Continue from the current place: the heroes need to hold a heavy door together and decide how to wait for reinforcements. Take into account the state of their arms, the weapons, the remaining charges, the availability of the technique and what each of them knows. Do not repeat the whole story.
n36.text:
2026-08-02 08:15

The oak door of the Upper Customs House closed with a heavy thud, and at once the bad news came out: the bar with which it was barred from inside had long since been carried off; the brackets were empty. There remained a mortise lock with a mechanical bolt, old and clogged with paint. Sava crouched down to it with the lockpick and said she would turn it, but she needed two minutes, maybe even three.

The first sentinel reached the door sooner. The blow landed in the middle of the leaf, and it gave by a palm's width.

"Everyone to the door!" Elin ordered. "Tarek, in the middle, shield and shoulder. I'm on your right, right shoulder and back. I don't push with my left arm, that's not up for discussion. Master healer, you're on the left, down low, feet against the threshold. Sava, your hands are needed by the lock, not by the planks."

The three of them leaned in. Tarek braced his shield against the leaf; the blue-handled dagger stayed in the sheath on his hip: there was no one to stab through oak. Elin pressed her right side to the door, keeping her freshly bandaged left arm at her chest, well away from the planks. The healer, grunting, sat down with his back to the leaf and dug his heels in against the threshold. From the depths of the arch the salt boiler from earlier ran up and silently took his place beside him. The door went back into place. The next blow they took as four and held.

"Now, how we wait," said Elin between blows, evenly, as if at guard mount. "We count what we have. Tarek has the dagger, and the shield as well. Sava has the lockpick and a short blade. I'm unarmed; I have a bracelet with three charges: one seal, and not before eight twenty. It's eight fifteen now. The company from the citadel has set out or is setting out; when it will arrive is unknown."

"Five minutes until the seal," said Tarek, taking a new blow on his shoulder. "I propose this: we hold the door with our bodies until Sava closes the lock. Then the lock holds, and we prop it in pairs and take turns, so we don't wear ourselves out."

"Accepted. And I'm not spending the seal just because eight twenty strikes. It's the last. It goes into action only if the door goes down before the company comes. If it goes down before eight twenty, we meet them in the arch with shield and blades, without it."

"And what if the company doesn't know we're here?" asked Sava, without looking up from the lock. The lockpick whirred in the keyhole. "Last night the whole west was silent, after all. I know why now, but in the citadel, will they hear today if anything happens?"

"They'll hear. Today the western bell is in working order and under guard; it hasn't been switched off a second time. And the courier left with my request at eight oh three, and the healer has confirmed that he got there. In the citadel they know where we are. Of the rest, not a word aloud: Roan is behind the door, he doesn't know about the night's business, and there's no reason to make him a gift of it."

The healer and the salt boiler exchanged glances, understood nothing and did not ask. Outside the blows suddenly stopped, and Roan's voice, muffled by the oak, calmly told someone to bring the log.

"Sava?" asked Elin.

"One more minute," she answered, and for the first time something in the lock gave with a dry click. Tarek shifted his feet, pressing into the shield, Elin braced her right shoulder harder, and all five waited for the next blow.
